When: The Scientific Secrets of Perfect Timing

Pink gathers research from psychology, biology and economics on timing to answer a practical question: when is the best time to do something? Your energy curve and “Suggested day” are built from this book's ideas.
Most people go through three phases each day: peak, trough and recovery. Morning and intermediate types follow roughly this order; evening types are close to the reverse.

At the peak, alertness is highest — good for focused, analytical work. In the trough, mistakes are most likely — good for routine tasks. In recovery, you're relaxed and less inhibited — good for creative, associative work.
Breaks are part of performance. Short, regular, screen-free breaks — walking, chatting, going outside — restore you better than pushing through.
The book suggests logging your energy at set times for several days to find your pattern from data rather than impressions.
The “idea time” in your report is the book's recovery phase: good ideas come most easily when your mind is relaxed. Log your energy for a few more days and your curve will get more accurate.

Bailey argues that the key to reaching goals isn't willpower or the latest productivity trick, but acting with more intention. Combining research on goal achievement, desire, values and procrastination with conversations with Buddhist monks, he lays out a path from values to daily action. Your values profile is organized around the book's 12 basic values.
The 12 basic values come from psychologist Shalom Schwartz's research, validated with hundreds of thousands of people in over eighty countries. Everyone holds all 12; only the weighting differs.

Values lie on two axes: preserving the status quo vs. making things better; focusing on yourself vs. on others. Neighboring values have similar motives; opposite values tend to pull against each other.
Every action is driven by a value. When a goal connects to what you value, it's easier to start and easier to finish.
Goals can be “edited”: some are worth keeping, some worth letting go.
The book mentions a few daily practices: intentional indulgence, knowing your opposing values, and checking which values your time goes to.

The report's values profile, value tensions and “ask yourself when stuck” all follow the book's 12 values and two axes. The author uses the formal PVQ-RR scale; this quiz is a simplified, self-made version meant for self-understanding.

Cirillo developed the Pomodoro Technique in the late 1980s while still a university student; it's named after the tomato-shaped kitchen timer he used. The method is simple: split time into blocks of focus and rest, so starting gets easier and your effort becomes visible.
One Pomodoro = 25 minutes of focus, then a 3–5 minute short break; after every 4 Pomodoros, take a longer break of about 15–30 minutes.
A Pomodoro can't be split. If interrupted, note it down and deal with it later; if you really must stop, that Pomodoro doesn't count — start over.
For outside interruptions: tell the person you're busy, agree to get back to them later, then follow up on time.
Record how many Pomodoros you finish each day, and use Pomodoro counts to estimate how much effort a task takes — your estimates will keep improving.
Fully step away from work during breaks so your brain recovers and the next Pomodoro stays focused.

The Pomodoro timer on “Today”, the long break every 4 Pomodoros, and the Pomodoro length suggested in your report all come from this method. Cirillo's standard is 25 minutes; adjust it to how long you can focus at a time.
